steps.action: Compared EROM-estimated discharge for all CONUS stream reaches with USGS gage and discrete-measurement locations, showing that small, low-flow streams are under-sampled.
steps.quote: are focused on streams of higher order, lower elevation, and with a greater flow than the average stream

steps.action: Posed three research questions on the accuracy, precision and suitable conditions of low-cost streamflow methods.
steps.quote: How accurate are low-cost streamflow gaging methods when compared with rated discharge from stable hydraulic controls under low flows?

steps.action: Collected published accuracies and precisions of the SF, RB, VR and current-meter methods as prior expectations.
steps.quote: Davids et al. (2019) reported the mean absolute percent errors (MAPEs) of 23%–63% in discharge for the SF method compared with an ADV.

steps.action: Took the VR head-velocity equation and the depth- and substrate-dependent surface velocity factors from the authors' earlier flume study.
steps.quote: were derived in a controlled laboratory flume setting (Hundt and Blasch 2019)

steps.action: Designed the test: sites at gaging stations with stable artificial weirs and flumes as the reference discharge, conventional plus low-cost methods at shared cross sections, 10 verticals, about 10 repeats each; conventional meters chosen by their share of NWIS measurements (Figure 2).
steps.quote: sites were chosen at existing USGS or U.S. Department of Agriculture Agricultural Research Service (ARS) streamflow gaging stations with artificial stable controls

steps.action: Set inclusion criteria for control stability, rating shifts, control condition and stage steadiness (<0.6 cm) during each measurement.
steps.quote: were considered stable if the maximum rate of change in survey levels was less than 0.003 m/year

steps.action: Made 275 field measurements (231 retained) by 20 people during 88 visits to 24 sites in eight states, with pebble counts for substrate class.
steps.quote: a total of 275 discharge measurements were made, 231 of which met project requirements

steps.action: Checked the rated-discharge reference by comparing conventional discrete measurements against it.
steps.quote: The conventional methods using all verticals produced median percent errors of less than or equal to 5%

steps.action: Computed percent error, RMSE, MAPE, bias and threshold fractions for each method against rated discharge (Table 4, Figure 6).
steps.quote: The low-cost methods had median percent errors less than 20%

steps.action: Subsampled the conventional measurements to 10 equally spaced verticals to estimate the error the 10-vertical protocol adds.
steps.quote: Subsetting the conventional measurements into 10 equally spaced verticals changed calculated discharge by 0.7% on average

steps.action: Characterized the precision of the low-cost methods from the standard deviations of repeat velocity measurements (Equation 8, Figure 7).
steps.quote: The SF and VR measurements were similar in precision, while RB measurements were less precise

steps.action: Recomputed discharge for all combinations of 1, 3, 7 and 10 verticals and 1 to 10 repeats to find the minimum effort that keeps 90% of estimates within 10% (Figures 8-10).
steps.quote: a minimum of three repeats at 10 verticals (30 velocity measurements) are required

steps.action: Compared the accuracies and precisions obtained here with Davids et al., Pike et al., Fonstad et al. and Hilgersom and Luxemburg.
steps.quote: Accuracies of the SF and VR methods are similar to previous field assessments.

steps.action: Recomputed SF and VR discharge under all-cobble and all-smooth substrate assumptions to bound the surface-velocity-factor uncertainty (Figure 11).
steps.quote: discharge was calculated for the SF and VR measurements assuming cobble substrates (Equation 3)

steps.action: Plotted the low-cost measurements against the paired conventional measurements as a second reference (supplement Figure S1).
steps.quote: the low-cost measurements are plotted against the corresponding conventional measurements in Figure S1

steps.action: Refined usage into depth, velocity and wind-dependent recommendations for each low-cost method (Table 5), drawing on the hydrographers' field experience and the results.
steps.quote: The SF method performs best when there is little to no wind and should be avoided when winds appear to affect the surface velocity.

steps.action: Kept the characterization: most conventional measurements fall within 5% and most low-cost measurements within 20%; SF is the most accurate and precise low-cost method.
steps.quote: were accurate within 20% relative to discharge records from stable, artificial hydraulic controls

end.claim: Low-cost surface float, rising body and velocity head rod methods give discharge mostly within 20% of rated discharge at stable controls in small streams (SF best: median absolute error 14%, precision 11%), while conventional meters are mostly within 5%.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing each method's discrete discharge with rated discharge from stable artificial hydraulic controls across 231 measurements produced the accuracy figures that make up the claim.

gates.evidence: Data acquisition was directed by descriptive research questions, not a stated hypothesis (p. 1512). The accuracy figures could have come out poor, but no acceptance threshold was set in advance; the 20% statement is descriptive (p. 1528). Site criteria and the 90%-within-10% threshold are reported in the Methods (pp. 1516, 1519) with no statement that they were fixed before the data were seen.

novelty_claims.quote: While no other studies have been found that evaluate the accuracy of this specific RB method deployed in the field
unlike many prior comparative studies, the measurement sites for this study were selected specifically to be adjacent to engineered control structures
the geographic scope and number of individuals performing the measurements are large for this type of comparative study

limits: No review file or earlier version was supplied, so there is no review sequence. The paper states no rival hypotheses; it is a benchmark characterization of existing methods against a field reference. none_fits is coded because no listed composition matches a reference-benchmark design: it is not capability_first (the methods are old and the question comes first) and not a trace series. Sub-claims and their statuses: SF most accurate and precise among the low-cost methods (capability_characterized); minimum repeats and verticals of 30/70/40 measurements (capability_characterized, within the sampled channels); condition-dependent recommendations in Table 5 (best_explanation at most, since they rest partly on hydrographers' qualitative field impressions and no wind data were collected, p. 1525). Conventional sample sizes are small for PAA (6) and PP (11). Precision was assessed only for the low-cost methods. Depth bias from yard sticks could not be analyzed (p. 1526). The rated 'truth' carries its own uncertainty (p. 1526). Inference: the site screening thresholds were presumably applied after data collection (44 of 275 measurements were excluded), but the timing is not stated.

disagreements.target: Turnipseed and Sauer (2010) guidance on float travel distance (about 40 s of travel)
disagreements.support: The authors spaced tag lines 0.6-1.2 m apart to avoid float migration toward the highest velocity under low-flow conditions.
disagreements.quote: This approach differs from the guidance under flooding conditions of Turnipseed and Sauer (2010)

disagreements.target: Davids et al. (2019), single surface velocity factor of 0.8
disagreements.support: Using depth- and substrate-dependent factors gave both positive and negative biases, unlike the positive biases Davids et al. report.
disagreements.quote: Davids et al. (2019) employed a single surface velocity factor of 0.8 for all measurements and report positive mean biases

disagreements.target: Pike et al. (2016) VR accuracy and Fonstad et al. (2005) VR precision
disagreements.support: This study's VR accuracy (19.6%) and precision (12%) are worse than those reported, which the authors attribute to differences in rod design and application.
disagreements.quote: an improvement in accuracy over the 19.6% found in this study

disagreements.target: Traditional guidance on surface velocity factors (Rantz 1982; Turnipseed and Sauer 2010)
disagreements.support: Surface velocity factors computed here (0.5-0.92, median 0.68) fall below the 0.84-0.90 range in the guidance, which the authors attribute to low-flow versus flood conditions.
disagreements.quote: includes values that are lower than a typical range of 0.84 for natural channels to 0.90 for concrete-lined channels

disagreements.support: Subsetting conventional measurements to 10 verticals changed discharge by 0.7% on average, so 10 verticals minimally affected accuracy at these sites.
disagreements.quote: Rantz (1982) recommended measuring velocity at 25 to 30 verticals
